Performance against base R and stringi

Source: vignettes/articles/benchmarks.Rmd
benchmarks.Rmd

This article compares zuregex with base R’s perl = TRUE functions and with stringi on eight common tasks. It is for readers deciding whether the speed difference matters for their data. The numbers come from one machine. Read them as ratios, not as times you will see.

How it was measured

The input is 50,000 synthetic log lines of about 64 ASCII characters. These are the first two; half the lines have a phone number and half end in no phone.

login user id=662153 user447@host6.com beta; warn, call 555-5110
delta beta id=633215 user22@host50.com beta; info, call 555-5676

Each task runs the same pattern through the three packages. The script first checks that all three give the same result, then times each with bench::mark() and keeps the median. One case is a single string, where the cost of the call itself dominates.

The machine was Intel(R) Core(TM) i5-8500B CPU @ 3.00GHz (x86_64-apple-darwin20), running R version 4.6.2 (2026-10-29), on 2026-11-16. It had zuregex 0.1.0 with PCRE2 10.49 and its JIT compiler, base R’s own PCRE2 10.47 2025-10-21, and stringi 1.8.9 with ICU 71.1. zuregex ran on 1 thread.

Results

Median time per call, in milliseconds. The two right-hand columns say how many times longer the other package took than zuregex, so a value above 1 means zuregex was faster.

Task Input zuregex base R stringi base R / zuregex stringi / zuregex
Detect 50,000 strings 10.338 12.018 34.136 1.2 3.3
Count matches 50,000 strings 18.612 327.303 45.882 17.6 2.5
Locate the first match 50,000 strings 11.429 19.525 46.392 1.7 4.1
Extract every match 50,000 strings 45.833 768.996 78.337 16.8 1.7
Capture groups 50,000 strings 21.058 1003.548 52.621 47.7 2.5
Replace every match 50,000 strings 30.364 41.815 87.535 1.4 2.9
Split 50,000 strings 32.859 54.504 58.067 1.7 1.8
Detect, one string 1 string 0.013 0.021 0.013 1.6 1.0

The pattern for each task:

Task zuregex base R stringi
Detect re_detect() grepl() stri_detect_regex()
Count matches re_count() gregexpr(), then counting stri_count_regex()
Locate the first match re_locate() regexpr() stri_locate_first_regex()
Extract every match re_extract_all() gregexpr() and regmatches() stri_extract_all_regex()
Capture groups re_match() utils::strcapture() stri_match_first_regex()
Replace every match re_replace() gsub() stri_replace_all_regex()
Split re_split() strsplit() stri_split_regex()
Detect, one string re_detect() grepl() stri_detect_regex()

Reading the numbers

The difference from base R is largest where base R needs two steps, a search and then R code that turns its offsets into counts, strings or columns: counting, extracting and capturing. strcapture() takes both steps inside one call. zuregex builds those results in C. Where base R also takes one call, as with grepl(), regexpr(), gsub() and strsplit(), the two are much closer.

On a single string the call itself dominates, so the three packages are within 10 microseconds of each other. zuregex keeps compiled patterns in a cache, so a pattern used again is not compiled again.

What the numbers do not show

  • Other machines give other ratios. The package’s own timing tests record that re_detect() was 0.6 times as fast as grepl() on an arm64 Mac, and that short calls run 10 to 25% behind base R on Linux, where base R’s call costs less. The two-step tasks were not measured elsewhere.
  • More threads change the large cases. These results are for one thread. On a machine with OpenMP, zuregex matches large inputs on several threads; re_threads() sets the cap.
  • Patterns differ. One corpus of short ASCII lines and four patterns is a small sample. Time your own patterns on your own data before you rely on a ratio.

Run it yourself

The script is tools/bench/run.R in the source repository. It needs stringi and bench. Run it against an installed build, because devtools::load_all() compiles without optimisation:

R CMD INSTALL --preclean --library=/tmp/zr-bench .
Rscript tools/bench/run.R /tmp/zr-bench

It writes vignettes/articles/benchmarks.csv, which this article reads.

See also

  • Move from base R and stringr maps each base R function to its zuregex verb.
  • ?re_threads and ?re_cache_size describe the two settings that most affect speed.
